worldSentence: The same energy disruption is now testing ships, household prices and corporate balance sheets, while a record crypto theft shows that digital scale can concentrate risk just as sharply as physical chokepoints do.
standfirst: Saturday's edition leads in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran says four tankers struck mines as a Qatari delegation returned to Tehran. Binance is absorbing a record breach, refining has become the profit centre at Exxon and Chevron, and Europe's economy is proving more resilient than expected. Curiosity Corner finds a third form of magnetism; the Long View visits fifteenth-century Melaka, where a port made strangers legible to one another.

connected.title: Today's common thread is concentrated infrastructure risk.

signals.label: HORMUZ
signals.text: Iran says four tankers struck mines on Friday; independent confirmation remains incomplete.

signals.label: BINANCE
signals.text: A hot-wallet breach became the largest known crypto theft, with about $3 billion frozen so far.

signals.label: REFINING
signals.text: Exxon's energy-products profit slightly exceeded upstream profit as fuel-making capacity tightened.

signals.label: EURO AREA
signals.text: Quarterly output beat expectations despite the energy shock, though the flash estimate is preliminary.

connected.note: A chokepoint, an exchange wallet and a refinery are very different systems, but each can become a point where large flows depend on a small number of controls. The useful distinction is between scale and resilience. Scale lowers ordinary costs; resilience determines what happens when the concentrated node fails, closes or is attacked.

stories.title: Four tankers were reported hit in the Strait of Hormuz as Qatar returned to Tehran for another diplomatic push.
stories.changed: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said four tankers struck mines and caught fire on Friday; Oman confirmed evacuating 25 crew from one burning tanker, while Iranian media said a Qatari delegation had arrived in Tehran for talks.
stories.matters: The shipping incidents raise the immediate cost and uncertainty of moving energy through the Gulf just as Qatar is testing whether reciprocal steps can prevent another round of U.S.-Iran strikes.
stories.watch: Vessel identities, independent evidence of what caused the explosions, insurer and shipping responses, and whether the Tehran visit produces a verified sequence on inspections, sanctions or the blockade. The fires and Omani rescue are confirmed; Iran's account of four mine strikes and the outcome of mediation are not independently established.

group.label: The lead
group.title: Physical danger and diplomacy have arrived in the same narrow waterway.
group.note: The urgent facts concern crews and ships; the strategic question is whether the incidents accelerate a deal or harden the parties' positions.

background.title: The incidents are serious, but the evidence remains uneven
background.text: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil and three other tankers struck mines after using what Tehran called unauthorised routes. It did not identify the vessels or crews, and the Associated Press could not independently verify that account. Oman separately said it evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker burning 1.6 nautical miles off Musandam. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre reported a vessel hit by an unknown projectile farther east, with its crew safe; it is not yet clear whether these reports describe the same incidents. The information gap matters because cause determines response: a mine, projectile, accident or enforcement action carries a different legal and military meaning. What is already clear is that operators face more than a theoretical risk in the strait.
background.known: The fires, an Omani rescue and the Qatari delegation's visit are confirmed through official or multiple reports.
background.new: Iran says four ships struck mines in one day; vessel identities, causes and links among the reported incidents remain uncertain.

left.label: Confirmed
left.text: Oman evacuated 25 crew from a burning tanker; Qatari mediators returned to Tehran.

right.label: Unverified
right.text: Iran's claim that four tankers hit mines after ignoring route instructions, and whether the incidents are connected.

sources.label: Associated Press · tanker incidents, Omani rescue and Qatar's Tehran visit

stories.title: Hackers removed about $6.3 billion from Binance in twenty minutes, exposing the industry's largest known custody failure.
stories.changed: Binance said attackers drained its own hot wallets across ten blockchains, roughly $3 billion has been frozen, withdrawals remain paused and the company has reserved more than $6.34 billion to cover the loss.
stories.matters: The incident is large enough to test whether an exchange can prove reserves, restore withdrawals and absorb a catastrophic operational loss without transferring it to customers or destabilising connected markets.
stories.watch: The promised proof-of-reserves snapshot, phased withdrawal restoration, recovery of unfrozen assets and a technical post-mortem. The loss and response are company-confirmed; attribution to a North Korean unit is a high-confidence assessment by blockchain firms, not a completed law-enforcement finding.

group.label: Technology & finance
group.title: The largest crypto theft is now a live test of custody, liquidity and proof.
group.note: A blockchain can record every movement and still leave the operational keys around it dangerously concentrated.

background.title: The breach hit connected operational wallets, not the ledger itself
background.text: Binance says the attack began at about 20:05 UTC on Thursday and moved approximately $6.3 billion of tokens out of hot wallets used to process transactions. Its first investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps laptop and access to a service container, but the company later said it had found additional points of compromise. It says there is no evidence that wallet private keys leaked and that customer balances were not directly taken. Those are preliminary company findings. The exchange has paused withdrawals, revoked affected authorisations and promised to replace all stolen assets using its SAFU reserve and corporate funds. It says about $5 billion is already held in the same tokens and about $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen with partners. The incident therefore shifts quickly from theft to verification: users need evidence that reserves match liabilities and that withdrawals can resume safely.
background.known: Binance confirmed a roughly $6.3 billion hot-wallet loss, paused withdrawals and committed company funds to cover it.
background.new: The exchange says most replacement assets are already assembled and a proof-of-reserves update is due Monday; neither the root cause nor full recovery is settled.

left.label: Containment
left.text: About $3bn frozen on-chain; affected authorisations revoked; withdrawals temporarily paused.

right.label: Unresolved
right.text: Roughly $3.3bn remains unfrozen, the full attack path is unknown and attribution is not official.

stories.title: Refining became the profit centre at Exxon and Chevron as wars tightened supplies of finished fuels.
stories.changed: Exxon earned $7.2 billion from energy products, slightly more than upstream, while Chevron's downstream profit reached $4.9 billion and U.S. refineries ran at record or near-record rates.
stories.matters: The earnings show where the energy shock is now biting: not only in crude supply, but in the capacity to turn crude into diesel, jet fuel and gasoline. That shifts profit toward refiners while raising costs for transport and households.
stories.watch: Restoration of Saudi and Russian refining capacity, Hormuz flows, fuel inventories and whether the majors spend the windfall on throughput, debt or distributions. Quarterly profits are reported; how long the margin regime lasts is unknown.

group.label: Economy & markets
group.title: The shortage has moved downstream from barrels to usable fuels.
group.note: Crude price alone no longer describes the constraint; refining capacity and product mix now determine who captures the margin.

background.title: Damaged capacity made finished fuels scarce enough to rival upstream economics
background.text: The wars involving Iran and Russia have disrupted crude flows and removed fuel-making capacity at a time of high transport demand. Exxon reported adjusted quarterly earnings of $17.5 billion and said its energy-products business earned $7.2 billion, marginally above upstream. Chevron reported $10.4 billion of adjusted earnings, with downstream profit of $4.9 billion and record U.S. crude throughput at 98% utilisation. Both companies are using part of the cash surge to reduce debt rather than immediately enlarge payouts: Exxon cut debt by $8 billion in the quarter and Chevron's net debt is nearly $14 billion lower than at the end of 2025. That is a capital-allocation signal as much as an earnings result. Management teams are treating the windfall as volatile, even while considering incremental refinery capacity and efficiency investments.
background.known: Both majors beat profit expectations as refining margins and utilisation surged; downstream earnings reached multi-year highs.
background.new: Exxon's energy-products profit exceeded upstream for the first time in at least six years, while both firms prioritised balance-sheet repair.

left.label: Exxon
left.text: $17.5bn adjusted earnings; $7.2bn energy-products profit; $8bn quarterly debt reduction.

right.label: Chevron
right.text: $10.4bn adjusted earnings; $4.9bn downstream profit; 98% U.S. refinery utilisation.

sources.label: Reuters · refining margins, segment mix and balance-sheet choices
Chevron · third-quarter results and operating measures

stories.title: The euro area grew 0.4% in the third quarter—twice the expected pace—despite the energy shock.
stories.changed: Eurostat's flash estimate put quarterly euro-area growth at 0.4% and annual growth at 1.3%, with Germany up 0.2%, Spain up 0.6%, Italy flat and France down 0.1%.
stories.matters: Europe is absorbing higher energy costs better than forecast, leaving the ECB with less reason to protect growth if inflation requires tighter policy.
stories.watch: The fuller 13 November estimate, fourth-quarter surveys and December's ECB meeting. The aggregate is official but preliminary, and Ireland's volatile 5.5% increase amplified the headline.

group.label: World beyond the lead
group.title: Europe is slowing, but it has not broken under the energy shock.
group.note: Resilience is not immunity: growth cooled from the second quarter and the inflation cost remains ahead.

radar.label: Curiosity Corner
radar.title: Physicists have experimentally confirmed a third kind of magnetism whose internal order is stable yet still readable.
radar.text: A SLAC-led team used X-rays to detect the handed, or chiral, spin structure predicted for altermagnets. Their spins alternate so the material has no net magnetisation, like an antiferromagnet, but the surrounding crystal geometry lets it generate spin-polarised currents, a useful feature of ferromagnets. The work confirms a material phase proposed only in 2022; faster memory and lower-power computing are possibilities, not demonstrated products.

radar.label: Qatar restaurant operations
radar.title: QSTP and talabat grow are pairing local restaurants with startups around logistics, supply chains and efficiency.
radar.text: The programme is designed to start with operating problems identified by restaurants rather than technology looking for a use. No participating companies, pilots or measured outcomes were disclosed, so the immediate value is the mechanism: give startups a live test environment and operators a structured route to evaluate tools under pressure.

radar.label: Qatar aviation
radar.title: Qatar Airways resumes twice-weekly Doha–Taif service today as its Saudi network rebuild continues.
radar.text: The Wednesday-and-Saturday route begins with QR1206 from Doha and joins the recently restored Qassim service. It is a modest capacity addition rather than a system-wide signal, but the sequence matters: the carrier is rebuilding secondary Saudi connectivity selectively while regional security and fuel costs remain unsettled.

attention.title: Open Binance's own incident update because the next test is verifiability, not reassurance.
attention.text: The notice separates preliminary cause, confirmed loss, frozen assets, customer impact and promised proof-of-reserves work. Reading the company claim beside the independent AP account makes clear what is known and what still depends on Binance producing evidence.

ignore.title: Ignore the race to declare the Binance attacker with certainty.
ignore.text: Two blockchain-intelligence firms assess a North Korean unit as the likely culprit, but Binance and U.S. authorities have not completed attribution. The operational failure, reserve coverage and withdrawal restoration can be evaluated before the identity claim is settled.

history.title: Melaka became a world port by making strangers legible to one another.
history.deck: Opposing monsoon winds brought merchants to the same narrow strait, but geography alone could not make them trade. Fifteenth-century Melaka built officials, law, weights, taxes and diplomatic protection around the wait—and turned a small port into the hinge between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.
history.thesis: Trade hubs win not merely by sitting on a route, but by reducing the uncertainty of using it. Melaka converted a seasonal meeting point into a market by organising difference: harbourmasters understood distinct merchant communities, maritime law governed ships and predictable duties made exchange easier to price.

sections.title: The monsoon created a market that had to wait
sections.text: Around 1400, Parameswara and his followers established Melaka near the narrowest passage between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. The location was powerful because opposing monsoon systems met there. Ships from India and the western ocean could arrive on one seasonal wind, while vessels from China and the archipelago arrived on another. Cargoes therefore had to pause, transfer and wait for the wind to reverse. That waiting time created an opportunity for an entrepôt: a place where Indian cloth, Chinese porcelain and silk, Sumatran pepper, Moluccan spices, Malay tin and regional food supplies could be warehoused and exchanged without one ship completing the entire journey. Geography produced traffic. It did not guarantee that merchants would choose Melaka over competing ports.

sections.title: Four harbourmasters made a cosmopolitan port administrable
sections.text: At its height, Melaka appointed four shahbandars, or harbourmasters, each responsible for merchant communities from particular regions. Foreign traders lived in separate districts, and their shahbandar arranged unloading, collected duties, checked weights and measures and represented their needs to the ruler. The design acknowledged that a single official could not credibly understand every language, custom and commercial practice in a city of Gujaratis, Tamils, Javanese, Chinese, Arabs, Persians and others. Melaka did not eliminate difference; it gave difference an interface. The officials were often drawn from foreign communities themselves, creating a layer of trusted translation between merchants and the state.

sections.title: Law extended trust from the quay onto the ship
sections.text: The Undang-Undang Melaka governed conduct in the city, while its maritime section, the Undang-Undang Laut Melaka, set rules for life and commerce aboard ships. It addressed authority, theft, quarrels and even the order in which goods could be traded after arrival. This mattered because a merchant voyage was both a transport service and a temporary society. Cargo owners, sailors and captains shared risk for months before reaching a court. By making expectations legible in advance, the code lowered the cost of bargaining after every dispute. Its influence later spread through maritime Southeast Asia, while Malay became a major language of coastal trade. Rules and language were network infrastructure as surely as warehouses were.

sections.title: Taxes were designed to keep the market supplied
sections.text: Melaka's rulers lived from commerce, but they did not charge every flow equally. Historical accounts describe basic import duties that varied by merchant origin, low charges on food imports and incentives for foreign traders to settle. The pattern reflected the port's dependence on other places: a wealthy trading city still needed rice, provisioning and permanent communities to function between sailing seasons. Revenue paid for the court, town and port, while predictable collection let merchants include duties in the economics of a voyage. This was not a frictionless free port, and rulers and officials also traded for their own account. Its achievement was to make extraction compatible, for a time, with repeat use of the market.

sections.title: Conquest showed that controlling a harbour is not the same as owning a network
sections.text: Portugal captured Melaka in 1511, seeking the choke point that connected the spice trade to the wider world. The fortress changed political control, but it did not compel merchants to preserve the old pattern. Many Muslim traders redirected business toward Johor and Aceh, while the displaced sultanate continued to contest Portuguese rule. The network could route around a port whose governance had become less acceptable to key participants. Melaka's rise and fall reveal the same principle from opposite directions. Location attracted traffic; institutions converted traffic into a trusted market; and when trust fractured, geography could not prevent commerce from finding alternatives.

timeline.text: Parameswara establishes Melaka near the narrow passage linking the Indian Ocean and South China Sea.
Relations with Ming China strengthen the port's diplomatic position and merchant traffic.
The sultanate expands influence and develops the administrative and legal machinery of a major port.
Melaka reaches its commercial height, served by four shahbandars and diverse resident merchant communities.
A Portuguese fleet arrives seeking direct access to the Asian spice trade.
Afonso de Albuquerque captures the port; significant merchant traffic shifts toward rival centres.
